title: Kisor v. Wilkie
lead: A veteran’s request for benefits dating to his original application turns on new service records and an agency’s interpretation of “relevant.”

actors.name: Kisor
actors.role: Vietnam veteran seeking retroactive disability benefits.

actors.name: Department of Veterans Affairs and Board of Veterans’ Appeals
actors.role: Agency and adjudicator interpreting the service-record reconsideration rule.

actors.name: Secretary Wilkie
actors.role: Government respondent defending the benefit decision.

proceedings: The agency denied the 1982 claim, reopened it in 2006, and awarded benefits from reopening.
The Veterans Court affirmed; the Federal Circuit deferred to the Board’s reading of its regulation.
The Supreme Court unanimously vacated and remanded, with five Justices retaining Auer under strengthened limits.
limits: The Court did not finally construe “relevant” or determine retroactive benefits. The five-vote deference limits and stare decisis rationale differ from Kagan’s four-vote defenses of delegation, the APA, and constitutionality.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: An original diagnosis denial precedes later supporting records
sections.cue: Why did the effective date remain disputed?
paragraphs: Kisor, a Vietnam veteran, applied in 1982 for disability benefits alleging post-traumatic stress disorder, or PTSD, linked to Operation Harvest Moon. A Veterans Affairs psychiatrist acknowledged his participation but did not diagnose PTSD, and benefits were denied.

In 2006 Kisor reopened the claim with a new psychiatric report and additional service records. The Department of Veterans Affairs, or VA, granted benefits from reopening. A regulation allowed reconsideration when relevant official service-department records had not previously been considered. Through one administrative judge, the Board of Veterans’ Appeals read “relevant” to require bearing on the reason for the earlier denial. The service records confirmed already-undisputed combat participation rather than supplying the formerly missing diagnosis. Kisor argued that relevance to another eligibility criterion sufficed even when that criterion had not been disputed.

sections.title: The Federal Circuit defers after finding both readings plausible
sections.cue: What did the Supreme Court agree to reconsider?
paragraphs: The Veterans Court affirmed. The Federal Circuit found both readings plausible and applied Auer deference because the Board’s interpretation was not plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulatory framework. The Supreme Court granted review to consider overruling Auer and Seminole Rock, the precedents governing deference to an agency’s reading of its own regulation. It did not undertake to decide Kisor’s entitlement or give a final construction itself.

sections.title: Five Justices require substantial interpretive work before deference
sections.cue: What must a reviewing court establish?
paragraphs: Kagan’s controlling framework required genuine ambiguity after exhausting text, structure, history, and purpose. Initial difficulty, technicality, or competing plausible assertions did not suffice. If those tools produced one reasonable meaning, courts had to enforce it; interpretation could not create a new regulation.

The agency’s reading then had to remain within the permissible range. The familiar plainly-erroneous formulation did not allow unlimited choice or a more indulgent reasonableness standard than the then-described Chevron regime.

Reasonableness was still insufficient. Courts had to assess authority, expertise, and fair considered judgment as important, nonexhaustive markers. An official position could come from appropriate staff and an authoritative vehicle without personal approval by the agency head. A casual employee view or disclaimed authority would not automatically qualify. Specialized expertise could inform technical or apparently ordinary policy questions, but an agency gained no advantage on familiar judicial questions, another agency’s domain, or statutory text merely copied into a regulation.

Convenient litigation positions, post hoc rationalizations, and unfair surprise ordinarily defeated deference. Surprise could arise from changed interpretations or retroactive treatment of long-unaddressed conduct. First appearances in briefs generally did not qualify, but Auer’s court-requested amicus position from a nonparty agency illustrated an exception. Without controlling deference, persuasive weight under Skidmore remained possible.

sources.pinpoint: Thresholds and further inquiry; Kagan majority slip 11–18 & nn.5–6

sections.title: Stare decisis preserves the doctrine, while broader defenses receive four votes
paragraphs: Roberts, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Sotomayor joined Kagan’s limits, stare decisis analysis, and disposition. The established line had shaped administrative law and settled regulatory constructions; Congress could alter its statutory foundations. Kisor showed no special justification such as unworkability or intervening legal change. Expansion of administration warranted firmer limits rather than abandonment.

Only Ginsburg, Breyer, and Sotomayor joined Kagan’s broader Parts II-A and III-A. She understood deference as a rebuttable presumption of delegated authority, drawing on agency knowledge of purposes, expertise, accountable policymaking, and uniformity. She read Administrative Procedure Act (APA) § 706 as not specifying a legal-review standard and § 553 as leaving interpretive explanations distinct from legislative rules: force came from the underlying regulation.

That plurality also disputed incentives for strategic vagueness and rejected separation-of-powers objections to the limited arrangement. Those APA and constitutional merits defenses did not receive Roberts’s fifth vote.

sources.pinpoint: Preserving Auer; Four-Justice rationale; Kagan slip 4–11,19–28

sections.title: The separate concurrences agree on remand but divide over Auer
sections.cue: How do persuasive expertise and controlling deference differ?
paragraphs: Roberts retained Auer on stare decisis grounds and emphasized practical overlap between qualified deference and persuasive, thorough, expert reasoning, while recognizing their conceptual difference. Statutory interpretation and Chevron were separate questions.

Gorsuch would abolish Auer. Thomas joined throughout, Kavanaugh Parts I–V, and Alito Parts I–III. Gorsuch disputed its historical origins and argued that independent judicial interpretation under § 706, rulemaking procedure under § 553, Article III, and impartial adjudication opposed controlling informal agency readings. He noted that Kisor’s own review statute, § 7292(d)(1), modeled APA commands; the suit did not directly arise under the APA.

In portions Alito did not join, Gorsuch rejected private authorial intent over public meaning, favored expertise as persuasion, disputed uniformity benefits, and distinguished methodological defaults from settled particular constructions for stare decisis. Kavanaugh, joined by Alito separately, also would retire Auer, expecting careful interpretation to resolve most cases. Open-ended rules expressly allowing policy choices instead called for State Farm review in his account, and statutory deference remained separate.

sources.pinpoint: Separate writings; Roberts slip 1–2; Gorsuch slip 1–42 & n.47; Kavanaugh slip 1–2

sections.title: The Federal Circuit must redo both ambiguity and authority analysis
paragraphs: The Federal Circuit had not exhausted the tools simply by recognizing two plausible positions. If ambiguity remained, it also needed to ask whether this single Board member’s nonprecedential decision expressed the agency’s considered authoritative view, a concern raised by the Solicitor General. The Court did not hold every Board decision categorically unqualified.

All nine Justices agreed to vacate and remand; five preserved Auer with limits and four favored overruling it. Kisor’s retroactive benefits and the regulation’s definitive meaning remained undecided. This historical 2019 judgment did not settle later disputes about statutory deference.
